blocks.etymology: From German Antisemitismus. It is typically said that German political agitator Wilhelm Marr invented the term to replace Judenhaß (literally “Jew-hatred”) to make hatred of the Jews seem rational and sanctioned by scientific knowledge; Marr founded the Antisemitenliga ("Anti-Semites' League") in 1879, used the terms Semitismus and Antisemiten in his 1879 and 1880 pamphlets Der Sieg des Judenthums über das Germanenthum and Der Weg zum Siege des Germanenthums über das Judenthum, and used Antisemitismus at least as early as his 1885 pamphlet Lessing contra Sem. The related term antisemitisch (“anti-semitic”) was first used in 1860, by Jewish scholar Moritz Steinschneider. See Wikipedia's article on the etymology and usage of the term. The term is superficially/synchronically equivalent to anti- + Semitism (see Semite), for which reason it is rarely extended to cover prejudice against any Semitic people, or against adherents of any of the religions that originated among the Semitic peoples (the Abrahamic religions). See the usage notes.

examples.vi: Nhiều nông dân dựa vào công nhân thời vụ trong đợt thu hoạch mùa hè.

examples.en: The restaurant updates its menu with seasonal fruits and vegetables.
examples.vi: Nhà hàng làm mới thực đơn của mình với các loại trái cây và rau củ theo mùa.

senses.vi: theo mùa; từng mùa; từng vụ

vi_block: Từng thời, từng lúc, từng mùa, từng vụ.

examples: It is a seasonal swimming pool.
wiktionary.gloss: Of, related to, or reliant on a season or period of the year, especially with regard to weather characteristics.

examples: Q: How's the weather there? A: The wind is pretty stiff, but it's seasonal, so no complaints.
wiktionary.gloss: Appropriate to the season.

senses.definition: a person employed only during a busy period of the year.

examples.en: The warehouse hired hundreds of seasonals before the holidays.
examples.vi: Nhà kho đã tuyển dụng hàng trăm lao động thời vụ trước kỳ nghỉ lễ.

blocks.etymology: From Middle English stepfader, from Old English stēopfæder, from Proto-Germanic *steupafadēr (“stepfather”), equivalent to step- + father. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Stäiffoar (“stepfather”), Dutch stiefvader (“stepfather”), German Low German Steevvader (“stepfather”), German Stiefvater (“stepfather”), Swedish styvfar (“stepfather”), Icelandic stjúpfaðir (“stepfather”).

senses.definition: The man who is married to your mother but is not your biological father.

examples.en: He gets along very well with his stepfather.

thesaurus.definition: the husband of your mother by a subsequent marriage

wiktionary.gloss: The husband of one's biological mother after her initial marriage to or relationship with one's biological father.
The husband of one's parent distinct from one's biological father or person with a similar relationship.

The form of a noun or pronoun used as the subject of a finite verb. In the active voice this is the agent, in the passive voice the subject is the receiver of the action. In both cases the subject is the thing subjected to what is said about it, it is the “topic of the statement”.

blocks.etymology: First attested in 1940, in John O'Hara's novel Pal Joey. The term is considered by the American Heritage Dictionary of Idioms, Second Edition (2013) and several other references to be a calque of German “was gibt's?” and/or a Yiddish equivalent. Brian Joseph disputes this, and speculates that despite extremely late attestation, it and the German was gibt's may "allow[] for a reconstruction of a Proto-West-Germanic existential use of 'give', which survives marginally into present usage."

examples: Not even thirty minutes after leaving the shower, my head starts itching. What gives?
wiktionary.gloss: What is wrong? Why is this happening?

examples: What gives with you and Martha?
wiktionary.gloss: What is happening? What is going on?
How are you?
The sound of one who whimpers; a whimper; a feeble complaint.
